analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal investigations of police misconduct and funds non-police safety programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with 9 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would beef up a Justice Department tool used since 1994 to investigate police departments that show a pattern of unconstitutional conduct, and to fix them through court-enforced agreements called consent decrees. It would require the Justice Department to include community oversight boards made up of people who have never worked in law enforcement, and to consider remedies beyond police reform, such as mental health services. It would also extend the law to cover prosecutors and judges, let state attorneys general bring their own investigations, and authorize roughly $595 million a year — $445 million for federal civil rights enforcement and $150 million in grants to states, including money for social workers and crisis teams as alternatives to police.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of cities and towns whose police departments fall under federal investigation would gain independent community oversight of court-enforced reforms, and communities generally would gain faster, better-funded investigations and state-level enforcement as a backup when the federal government does not act. States pursuing investigations could get grants to fund social workers, behavioral health crisis experts, and alternatives to police enforcement of traffic rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Justice Department to modify consent decree procedures to include community oversight bodies composed of people who have never worked in law enforcement, with authority to question agencies, obtain documents, and recommend changes [S2].
Authorizes $445 million per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2034 for the Civil Rights Division, with at least $100 million per year reserved for pattern-or-practice enforcement [S2].

Expands the underlying civil rights statute to cover prosecutors, judges, and other justice-system officials, not just law enforcement officers, while protecting prosecutors' discretion to decline charges [S2].

Creates a new pathway for state attorneys general to bring their own pattern-or-practice lawsuits, with safeguards to prevent conflicts of interest, plus $150 million per year in grants to help states conduct investigations and fund non-police programs like social workers and behavioral crisis teams [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the federal treasury — up to roughly $595 million per year in authorized spending — and on police departments and justice-system agencies that would face broader investigations, court-enforced reforms, and independent community scrutiny.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes nearly $6 billion over ten years in new federal spending on top of existing Justice Department budgets, at a time of persistent budget pressure [S2].

Extending the pattern-or-practice statute to prosecutors and judges, even with a protection for charging discretion, could expose routine judicial and prosecutorial decisions to federal civil litigation, raising concerns about intrusion into the independence of the courts.

Consent decrees impose years of court supervision on local police agencies at significant cost to local budgets, and the bill directs the Justice Department to implement remedies expeditiously, which some officials argue can force changes faster than agencies can absorb them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities where police departments are found to have engaged in unconstitutional patterns of conduct, stronger investigations, community oversight, and funded alternatives to policing address problems the existing system has handled slowly and inconsistently. The costs — federal spending and compliance burdens on local agencies — are real but fall mainly on governments and agencies being held accountable. The main design risk is the extension to judges, which goes beyond police misconduct into territory courts may resist.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2024, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 22, 2024, with nine cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on May 22, 2024, and no further action appears in the record [S4].
The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, meaning it would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and justice-system agencies are better off: the broader investigations, community oversight boards, and expanded state enforcement authority never took effect. The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division also avoids the mandated $445 million annual funding floor and the requirement to open the door to state-led lawsuits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and their oversight resisters

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand federal pattern-or-practice investigations and fund community-based alternatives to policing.

for.name: Sens. Hirono, Duckworth, Wyden, Sanders, Merkley, Van Hollen, Booker, Welch, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it 10 total Senate sponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chair with authority to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee with no action after referral in May 2024.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to move a bill through committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors were Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill's death in committee split along the party lines visible in the sponsor list.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (police departments and sheriffs' offices)
industries.note: The bill widens the channel for federal and state pattern-or-practice investigations, mandates community oversight bodies with document access, and steers grant money away from police operations toward alternatives. Departments facing such investigations would lose the relative insulation of a slower, underfunded federal enforcement process.

industries.industry: Police unions and police professional associations
industries.note: Consent decrees and community oversight bodies constrain departments' control over discipline, staffing, and operations, and these groups have historically opposed such court-supervised reforms. The bill's machinery would strengthen that oversight in more jurisdictions.

industries.industry: Community behavioral health and crisis-response services
industries.note: State grants could fund social workers, behavioral health crisis experts, and non-police traffic enforcement, and consent decrees could require mental health support and restorative justice programs — new funding streams for community-based service providers.
